concept.name: Gamma exposure
concept.definition: Gamma exposure (GEX) is the aggregate gamma held by options market makers (dealers) across strikes and expirations, typically expressed in dollars of underlying per one-point or one-percent move. It estimates how much dealers must buy or sell in the underlying to re-hedge as the price moves, and its sign distinguishes volatility-dampening (long gamma) from volatility-amplifying (short gamma) regimes.
concept.intuition: Every option a dealer sells must be hedged with stock or futures; add up those hedges across the whole market and you get an estimate of the mechanical buying and selling that price moves themselves will trigger.
concept.mechanics: Dealers delta-hedge their option books, so their required hedge flow per unit move equals their net gamma: long gamma means selling into rallies and buying dips (stabilizing); short gamma means the reverse (destabilizing). Practitioners estimate GEX from open interest by strike with assumptions about dealer positioning; Cboe's own analysis of SPX 0DTE flow found customer activity balanced enough that net market-maker gamma was typically small relative to futures liquidity.
concept.formula: GEX per strike ~ gamma x open interest x contract multiplier x spot (per unit move); summed across strikes for total dealer gamma.
concept.failure_modes: GEX is an estimate built on unverifiable assumptions about who is long or short each series — Cboe notes outside observers cannot see the customer/dealer split, and published estimates for the same day have ranged from record short to +$50bn long. Treating GEX levels as precise magnets or guaranteed support/resistance is unsupported.
concept.misconceptions: High option volume does not mean high dealer gamma — if customer buying and selling are balanced, net dealer exposure is near zero regardless of notional traded. Nor does a 'gamma flip level' mechanically force price behavior; it summarizes positioning, not causation.
concept.example: If dealers are net long $2bn of SPX gamma per 1% move, a 1% rally obliges them to sell roughly $2bn of futures to stay hedged — flow that leans against the move; Cboe measured typical 0DTE net gamma at only 0.04%-0.17% of daily S&P futures liquidity.

citations.source: Cboe — Volatility Insights: Evaluating the Market Impact of SPX 0DTE Options (Mandy Xu, 2023)
